rationale: Both warn a son against envying sinners; 24:1 also forbids desiring their company, while 23:17 redirects the heart toward reverence for the Lord.
source_text: Son, do not envy evil men, and do not desire to be with them;

target_texts.text: Do not let your heart envy sinners, but be in the fear of the Lord the whole day;

rationale: The evil companions' hearts meditate lies; the twisted heart in 6:14 likewise continually devises evils and produces civic disturbance.
source_text: for their heart meditates lies, and their lips speak toils.

target_texts.text: with a twisted heart he devises evils at every time. Such a person stirs up disturbances for a city.

rationale: Wisdom builds and establishes a house here; 9:1 personifies Wisdom as building her own house and setting its pillars.
source_text: With wisdom a house is built, and with understanding it is raised upright;

target_texts.text: Wisdom built herself a house, and set seven pillars beneath it.

rationale: Discernment fills storerooms with good wealth; Wisdom likewise promises substance and storehouses filled with good things to those who love her.
source_text: with discernment store-rooms are filled from every precious and good wealth.

target_texts.text: I walk in ways of righteousness, and move in the midst of paths of just judgment,
so that I may apportion substance to those who love me, and fill their storehouses with good things.

rationale: Both explicitly rank wisdom above strength; Ecclesiastes extends the comparison to weapons of war, illuminating this proverb's preference for understanding.
source_text: A wise person is better than a strong one, and a man with understanding than a great cultivated estate;

target_texts.text: I said, Wisdom is better than strength; yet the poor man’s wisdom is despised, and his words are not heard.
The words of the wise, heard quietly, are better than the shouting of rulers in follies.
Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner will destroy much good.

rationale: Both connect steering and counsel with deliverance: warfare needs deliberation here, while lack of steering causes a fall in 11:14.
source_text: with steering war takes place, and help is with a deliberative heart.

target_texts.text: Those who have no steering fall like leaves, but deliverance is in much counsel.

rationale: Wisdom is located at the gates of the wise here; the opening proclamation likewise places Wisdom publicly at rulers' gates and city gates.
source_text: Wisdom and good reflection are in the gates of the wise; the wise do not turn from the mouth of the Lord,

target_texts.text: Wisdom is celebrated at the exits, and in the squares she speaks openly.
At the tops of walls she is proclaimed; at rulers’ gates she sits nearby, and at city gates she speaks boldly:

rationale: In the continuing contrast with wise deliberation in 24:7, death meets the uneducated; 9:6 urges leaving foolishness and seeking understanding in order to live.
source_text: but deliberate in councils. Death meets the uneducated,

target_texts.text: Leave foolishness, and you will live; seek understanding, so that you may live, and set insight right in knowledge.”

rationale: The fool dies in sins here; 5:23 similarly describes an undisciplined person dying and perishing through folly.
source_text: and a fool dies in sins; and impurity will be defiled in a pestilent man,

target_texts.text: He dies among the undisciplined; from the abundance of his own life he was cast out and perished through folly.

rationale: The command to rescue people being led to death accords with Isaiah's demand to rescue the wronged and defend those exposed to injustice.
source_text: Rescue those being led to death, and ransom those being killed; do not hold back.

target_texts.text: Learn to do good, seek judgment, rescue the wronged. Give judgment for the orphan and vindicate the widow.

rationale: Both say that the Lord examines human hearts and repays each person according to conduct; professed ignorance cannot conceal responsibility from Him.
source_text: But if you say, “I do not know this person,” know that the Lord knows everyone’s hearts, and the One who fashioned breath for all Himself knows everything, and repays each one according to his works.

target_texts.text: I, the Lord, examine hearts and test kidneys, to give each according to his ways and the fruits of his practices.

rationale: The honey eaten here introduces the comparison with wisdom in 24:14; 16:24 similarly makes honeycomb sweetness an image of beneficial words.
source_text: Eat honey, son, for a honeycomb is good, so that your throat may be sweetened;

target_texts.text: Good words are honeycombs, and their sweetness is healing of the life.

rationale: Both describe a favorable future in which hope does not depart, here for the person who finds wisdom and there for keeping reverence toward the Lord.
source_text: in this way you will perceive wisdom for your own life; for if you find it, your end will be good, and hope will not abandon you.

target_texts.text: for if you keep these things, you will have offspring, and your hope will not depart.

rationale: The righteous falls and rises again; Micah likewise refuses an enemy's triumph because the fallen speaker will rise with the Lord's help.
source_text: for the righteous will fall seven times and rise, but the impious will grow weak amid evils.

target_texts.text: Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen! I will rise, for if I sit in darkness, the Lord will shine for me.

rationale: Both condemn rejoicing over another person's downfall; 17:5 states that delight in someone perishing will not go unpunished.
source_text: If your enemy falls, do not rejoice over him, and at his tripping do not lift yourself up,

target_texts.text: One who laughs at the poor provokes the One who made him, and one who rejoices over someone perishing will not be acquitted; but one who has compassion will receive mercy.

rationale: This reason for refusing triumph over a fallen enemy invokes the Lord's displeasure; 17:5 likewise places rejoicing at another's destruction under divine accountability.
source_text: for the Lord will see, and it will not please Him, and He will turn His wrath away from him.

target_texts.text: One who laughs at the poor provokes the One who made him, and one who rejoices over someone perishing will not be acquitted; but one who has compassion will receive mercy.

rationale: Both directly prohibit envy of sinners, directing the reader away from treating evildoers as desirable models.
source_text: Do not rejoice over evildoers, and do not envy sinners;

target_texts.text: Do not let your heart envy sinners, but be in the fear of the Lord the whole day;

rationale: Both portray the impious person's future through an extinguished light; 24:20 calls it a lamp and also denies enduring offspring.
source_text: for evil people will certainly have no offspring, and the lamp of the impious will be extinguished.

target_texts.text: Light is for the righteous continually, but the light of the impious is extinguished.

rationale: The paired command to fear God and respect the king is closely reflected in Peter's distinct commands to fear God and honor the king.
source_text: Fear God, son, and the king, and disobey neither of them;

target_texts.text: Honor everyone. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the king.

rationale: The warning about punishment follows obedience to God and king; Peter similarly connects submission to rulers with their punishment of evildoers.
source_text: for suddenly they will punish the impious, and who will know the punishments of both?

target_texts.text: Submit yourselves to every human institution for the Lord’s sake, whether to a king as supreme,
or to governors as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of those who do good.

rationale: Guarding the received word keeps a son outside destruction here; keeping a command likewise guards one's life in 19:16.
source_text: A son who guards a word will be outside destruction, and receiving it, he has received it.

target_texts.text: One who keeps a command guards his own life, but one who despises his own ways will perish.

rationale: The prohibition of false speech to a king corresponds to the king's approval of righteous lips and upright words in 16:13.
source_text: Let no falsehood from a tongue be spoken to a king, and no falsehood will ever come from his tongue.

target_texts.text: Righteous lips are acceptable to a king, and he loves upright words.

rationale: The king's tongue acts as a crushing sword here; 16:14 likewise describes royal wrath as a messenger of death.
source_text: A king’s tongue is a sword and is not made of flesh, and whoever is handed over will be crushed;

target_texts.text: A king’s wrath is a messenger of death, but a wise man will appease him.

rationale: The sharpened royal wrath consumes people here; 20:2 compares a king's threat to a lion's wrath and warns that provoking him endangers life.
source_text: for if his wrath is sharpened, it consumes human beings with their sinews,

target_texts.text: A king’s threat does not differ at all from a lion’s wrath, and one who provokes him sins against his own life.

rationale: The speaker disclaims human understanding instead of claiming wisdom for himself; 3:7 warns against considering oneself prudent.
source_text: For I am the most foolish of all people, and human understanding is not in me.

target_texts.text: Do not be prudent in your own estimation; fear God and turn away from every evil.

rationale: The native text positively says God taught the speaker wisdom; 2:6 likewise identifies the Lord as the giver of wisdom, knowledge, and understanding.
source_text: God has taught me wisdom, and knowledge of holy ones I have known.

target_texts.text: For the Lord gives wisdom, and from His presence come knowledge and understanding.

rationale: The question about ascending to heaven and descending has a close counterpart in John's statement about the Son of Man; the link concerns ascent and descent, not identification of every figure in Proverbs.
source_text: Who went up to heaven and came down? Who gathered winds in a fold of his garment? Who wrapped water in a cloak? Who took hold of all the ends of the earth? What is his name, or what is his children’s name, so that you may know?

target_texts.text: And no one has ascended into heaven except the One who descended from heaven, the Son of Man.

rationale: Both join God's fire-tested sayings with His protection of those who rely upon Him; Proverbs describes Him as shielding those who revere Him.
source_text: All God’s words have been refined by fire, and He shields those who revere Him.

target_texts.text: My God’s way is blameless; the Lord’s sayings are tried by fire; He is a protector of all who hope in Him.

rationale: Both prohibit adding to the divine word; Proverbs adds that doing so risks reproof and exposure as false.
source_text: Do not add to His words, so that He may not reprove you and you become false.

target_texts.text: You shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall you take away from it; you shall keep the commandments of the Lord your God, which I command you this day.

rationale: The prayer for neither wealth nor poverty but sufficient provision corresponds to contentment with food and coverings in First Timothy.
source_text: Put a vain and false word far from me; give me neither wealth nor poverty; assign me what is needed and sufficient,

target_texts.text: But godliness with contentment is great gain.
For we brought nothing into the world, because neither can we carry anything out.
But having food and coverings, with these we will be content.

rationale: Both warn that becoming full and prosperous can lead to forgetting or denying God; Proverbs also recognizes poverty's separate temptation to steal.
source_text: so that I may not become full and false and say, “Who sees me?” or become poor and steal and swear by the name of God.

target_texts.text: Take heed unto yourself, lest you forget the Lord your God, and fail to keep His commandments, and His judgments, and His ordinances which I command you this day;
lest, when you have eaten and are filled, and have built good houses and dwelt in them,
and your herds and your flocks are multiplied, and your silver and your gold are multiplied, and all that you have is multiplied,
you become lifted up in heart, and forget the Lord your God, who brought you forth out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage;

rationale: The offspring who curse their father and withhold blessing from their mother enact the opposite of the command to honor father and mother.
source_text: Evil offspring curse a father and do not bless the mother.

target_texts.text: Honour your father and your mother, that it may be well with you, and that your days may be long upon the good land which the Lord your God gives you.

rationale: A generation declares itself righteous despite remaining unclean; 20:9 similarly challenges anyone's confident claim to a pure heart and freedom from sins.
source_text: Evil offspring judge themselves righteous, but have not washed away their discharge.

target_texts.text: Who will boast that he has a pure heart? Or who will speak confidently of being clean from sins?

rationale: Lofty eyes and self-exalting eyelids embody the pride condemned in 16:5, where everyone high of heart is unclean before God.
source_text: Evil offspring have lofty eyes and exalt themselves with their eyelids.

target_texts.text: Everyone high of heart is unclean before God, and one who unjustly puts hands into a hand will not be acquitted.

rationale: Both picture oppressors as consuming people: swordlike teeth devour the poor here, while Micah portrays rulers stripping flesh and crushing bones.
source_text: Evil offspring have swords for teeth and cutting blades for molars, to consume and devour the lowly from the earth and their poor from among people.

target_texts.text: He will say: “Hear these things now, authorities of Jacob’s house and remaining ones of Israel’s house! Is it not for you to know justice,
you who hate good things and seek evil things, who snatch their skins from them and their flesh from their bones?”
Just as they ate the flesh of My people, flayed their skins from their bones, crushed their bones and divided them into pieces like flesh for a cauldron and meat for a cooking pot,

rationale: Both forbid partiality in judgment; Leviticus explicitly requires judging the neighbor righteously rather than favoring social position.
source_text: These things I say to you, the wise, to recognize: to show deference to a face in judgment is not good;

target_texts.text: You shall do no injustice in judgment; you shall not favour the person of the poor, neither shall you admire the person of the mighty; you shall judge your neighbour in righteousness.

rationale: Calling an impious person righteous is condemned in both passages; 17:15 also condemns the converse injustice of declaring the righteous unjust.
source_text: One who says of the impious, “He is righteous,” will be accursed among peoples and hated among nations;

target_texts.text: One who judges the unjust righteous and the righteous unjust is unclean and detestable before God.

rationale: Reprovers receive blessing here, while 28:23 promises greater favor to a person who reproves another's conduct than to a flattering speaker.
source_text: but those who reprove will appear better, and a good blessing will come upon them;

target_texts.text: One who reproves a person’s ways will have more favor than one who flatters with the tongue.

rationale: The warning against being a false witness to a fellow citizen restates the prohibition of false witness against one's neighbor.
source_text: Do not be a false witness against your fellow citizen, and do not make your lips wide;

target_texts.text: You shall not bear false witness against your neighbour.

rationale: Both reject personal repayment of injury; Romans explicitly forbids repaying evil for evil and reserves vengeance for the Lord.
source_text: Do not say, “As he treated me, I will treat him, and I will punish him for the wrong he did me.”

target_texts.text: Repay no one evil for evil. Take thought for what is honorable before all people.
If possible, as far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people.
Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but make room for wrath; for it is written, “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay, says the Lord.”

rationale: The comparison of the foolish person to a field and vineyard, developed in 24:31-34, resembles the idle person's thorn-strewn ways in 15:19.
source_text: A foolish man is like a cultivated field, and a person lacking understanding like a vineyard;

target_texts.text: The ways of the idle are strewn with thorns, but those of the courageous are well worn.

rationale: The overgrown and abandoned cultivation pictures the consequences of neglect; 15:19 similarly contrasts the idle person's thorns with the courageous person's usable ways.
source_text: if you leave him alone, he will become wasteland, and grow wild with grass all over and become abandoned, and his stone fences are torn down.

target_texts.text: The ways of the idle are strewn with thorns, but those of the courageous are well worn.

rationale: The observer reconsiders what he sees and chooses discipline; 22:3 likewise contrasts the resourceful person's instruction through observing punishment with fools who pass by unchanged.
source_text: Afterward I reconsidered; I looked so as to choose discipline.

target_texts.text: A resourceful person, seeing an evil person severely punished, is himself instructed, but fools passed by and were penalized.

rationale: Both repeat the lazy person's sequence of a little sleep, a little dozing, and hands clasped over the chest.
source_text: “A little I doze, a little I sleep, a little I clasp my chest with my hands”—

target_texts.text: You sleep a little, sit a little, doze a little, and clasp your chest with your hands a little;

rationale: Both personify poverty as arriving and want as a runner, making them the consequences of the preceding indulgence in sleep.
source_text: but if you do this, your poverty will come marching in front, and your want like a good runner.

target_texts.text: then poverty arrives beside you like an evil traveler, and want like a good runner.

rationale: The unfilled leech and the refusal to say enough introduce the list in 30:16; 27:20 likewise uses unfilled Hades and destruction to portray insatiable appetite.
source_text: The leech had three daughters, dearly loved, and these three did not fill her, and the fourth was not content to say, “Enough!”

target_texts.text: Hades and destruction are not filled, and likewise human eyes are insatiable.

rationale: Hades appears among things never filled in both passages; 27:20 applies the same insatiability to human eyes.
source_text: Hades and a woman’s desire, and Tartarus and land not filled with water, and water and fire will certainly not say, “It is enough.”

target_texts.text: Hades and destruction are not filled, and likewise human eyes are insatiable.

rationale: Both join dishonoring parents with punishment affecting the eyes: ravens peck them out here, while darkness overtakes the offending person's pupils in 20:9a.
source_text: An eye mocking a father and dishonoring a mother’s old age—may ravens from the ravines peck it out, and may young eagles devour it.

target_texts.text: The lamp of one who speaks evil of a father or mother will be extinguished, and the pupils of his eyes will see darkness.

rationale: The adulterous woman's claim to have done nothing improper resembles the generation that judges itself righteous despite uncleanness; both expose false self-acquittal.
source_text: Such is the way of an adulterous woman: when she has acted, she washes herself and says she has done nothing improper.

target_texts.text: Evil offspring judge themselves righteous, but have not washed away their discharge.

rationale: Both pair a fool enjoying material abundance with a household servant raised to rule, presenting these reversals as unfitting or disruptive.
source_text: if a household servant becomes king, and a fool is filled with food,

target_texts.text: Luxury does not benefit a fool, nor does it benefit a household servant if he begins to rule with insolence.

rationale: The small creatures' exceptional wisdom corresponds to the bee's advancement through honoring wisdom despite bodily weakness in 6:8c.
source_text: Four things are smallest upon the earth, yet these are wiser than the wise:

target_texts.text: Although weak in bodily strength, she was advanced because she honored wisdom.

rationale: Both commend ants for preparing food in summer, using their practical foresight to teach wisdom beyond physical strength.
source_text: the ants, which have no strength, yet prepare their food in summer;

target_texts.text: Go to the ant, sluggard; see its ways and emulate them, and become wiser than it.
For although it has no cultivated field, and has no one forcing it, and is under no master,
it prepares its food in summer and makes abundant provision at harvest.

rationale: The rock badgers make homes in rocks here; the psalm similarly calls rock a refuge for rock rabbits, preserving the respective native animal wording.
source_text: and the rock badgers, a nation without strength, which made their own houses in rocks;

target_texts.text: The high mountains are for deer; a rock is a refuge for rock rabbits.

rationale: The locusts march in order despite having no king; Joel's advancing force likewise keeps individual paths and coordinated ranks. This is an image comparison, not an identification of the force.
source_text: the locust is without a king, yet marches out in good order at one command;

target_texts.text: Like fighters they will run, and like soldiers they will climb the walls. Each will go on his own road, and they certainly will not turn aside from their paths,
and no one will hold back from his brother. Burdened with their weapons they will go, and among their missiles they will fall, yet they will certainly not be destroyed.

rationale: The native warning links fighting with dishonor, while 20:3 calls withdrawal from abuse honorable and describes fools as becoming entangled in it.
source_text: If you give yourself over to merriment and stretch out your hand with fighting, you will be dishonored.

target_texts.text: It is glory for a man to turn away from abuse, but every fool entangles himself in such things.

rationale: Dragging out words produces disputes as squeezing nostrils produces blood; 15:1 likewise says painful speech stirs anger, contrasting a yielding answer.
source_text: Milk out milk, and there will be butter; but if you squeeze nostrils, blood will come out; and if you drag out words, disputes and battles will come out.

target_texts.text: Anger destroys even intelligent people; but a yielding answer turns away wrath, and a painful word stirs up anger.

rationale: A king receives instruction from his mother here; 1:8 explicitly commands the son not to reject his mother's ordinances.
source_text: My words have been spoken by God, an oracle concerning a king whom his mother instructed.

target_texts.text: Listen, son, to your father’s discipline, and do not reject your mother’s ordinances,

rationale: The mother calls her son to keep God's sayings; 6:20 similarly instructs the son to guard paternal laws and retain maternal ordinances.
source_text: What will you keep, child? What? God’s sayings. Firstborn, I speak to you, son. What, child of my womb? What, child of my vows?

target_texts.text: Son, guard your father’s laws, and do not reject your mother’s ordinances.

rationale: The warning against giving wealth to women is sharpened by 29:3's specific warning that maintaining prostitutes destroys wealth; the target is a particular related danger.
source_text: Do not give women your wealth, or your mind and livelihood to belated counsel.

target_texts.text: When a man loves wisdom, his father rejoices; but one who tends prostitutes will destroy wealth.

rationale: The instruction that the powerful avoid wine accords with 20:1's association of wine and drunkenness with lack of discipline, insolence, and loss of wisdom.
source_text: Do everything with counsel; drink wine with counsel. The powerful are hot-tempered, but let them not drink wine,

target_texts.text: Wine is undisciplined, and drunkenness insolent, and everyone who mingles with it will not be wise.

rationale: Both connect powerful men's drinking with corrupt judgment: forgetting wisdom and failing the weak here, and depriving the righteous of their rights in Isaiah.
source_text: so that, after drinking, they may not forget wisdom and become entirely unable to judge the weak rightly.

target_texts.text: Woe to your strong ones who drink wine and the powerful who mix strong drink,
who justify the ungodly for gifts and take away the righteous person’s right!

rationale: The native command is to speak God's word and judge everyone soundly; Leviticus supplies the corresponding requirement of righteous, impartial judgment.
source_text: Open your mouth for God’s word, and judge everyone soundly.

target_texts.text: You shall do no injustice in judgment; you shall not favour the person of the poor, neither shall you admire the person of the mighty; you shall judge your neighbour in righteousness.

rationale: Both call for active just judgment on behalf of vulnerable people: the poor and weak here, and the wronged, orphan, and widow in Isaiah.
source_text: Open your mouth and judge justly, and decide the case of the poor and weak.

target_texts.text: Learn to do good, seek judgment, rescue the wronged. Give judgment for the orphan and vindicate the widow.

rationale: The king's heart is beyond human examination here; Jeremiah likewise describes the human heart as deep and difficult to know, while distinguishing the Lord's searching knowledge.
source_text: Heaven is high and earth deep, but a king’s heart is beyond examination.

target_texts.text: The heart is deep beyond all things, and so is a human; and who will know him?
I, the Lord, examine hearts and test kidneys, to give each according to his ways and the fruits of his practices.

rationale: The cleansing of unapproved silver introduces removal of wickedness in 25:5; 17:3 also uses metal testing as an image for evaluating human hearts.
source_text: Beat unapproved silver, and it will be cleansed, entirely pure;

target_texts.text: As silver and gold are tested in a furnace, so hearts are chosen before the Lord.

rationale: Removing the impious makes the throne prosper in righteousness; 16:12 similarly grounds a throne's establishment in righteousness and royal rejection of evil.
source_text: Kill the impious from before a king, and his throne will prosper in righteousness.

target_texts.text: One who does evil is an abomination to a king, for a throne of rule is prepared with righteousness.

rationale: Both warn against taking an exalted place for oneself in an honored gathering, because a public demand to yield one's place brings humiliation.
source_text: Do not boast before a king, and do not station yourself in the places of rulers;

target_texts.text: “When someone invites you to a wedding feast, do not recline in the foremost place. Someone more honored than you may have been invited by him,
and the one who invited you both will come and say to you, ‘Give this man your place.’ Then you will begin, with shame, to occupy the last place.

rationale: The preferable invitation to come higher closely resembles the host's invitation in Luke, where voluntary humility leads to honor before others.
source_text: for it is better for you to be told, “Come up to me,” than for him to humble you before a ruler. Say what your eyes have seen.

target_texts.text: But when you are invited, go and recline in the last place, so that when the one who invited you comes, he will say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will have honor before all who recline at table with you.
For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted.”

rationale: The warning against rushing into battle corresponds to the honor of turning away from abuse and avoiding the fool's entanglement in conflict.
source_text: Do not rush quickly into battle, so that you do not regret it at the end. When your friend reproaches you,

target_texts.text: It is glory for a man to turn away from abuse, but every fool entangles himself in such things.

rationale: Withdrawing rather than showing contempt when a friend reproaches resembles the wise person's loving reception of reproof in 9:8.
source_text: withdraw backward; do not show contempt,

target_texts.text: Do not reprove evil people, so that they may not hate you; reprove a wise person, and he will love you.

rationale: The command to guard one's ways with readiness for reconciliation corresponds to Jesus' instructions to seek reconciliation and settle promptly with an adversary.
source_text: Favor and friendship set one free; keep these for yourself so that you do not become subject to reproach, but guard your ways with readiness to be reconciled.

target_texts.text: If therefore you offer your gift upon the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you,
leave your gift there before the altar, and go; first be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
Come to terms with your adversary quickly, while you are with him on the way, lest your adversary hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the officer, and you be thrown into prison.

rationale: A spoken word is compared to precious gold and carnelian here; 16:24 similarly uses a desirable material image, sweet honeycomb, to commend good words.
source_text: A golden apple on a carnelian necklace—so is speaking a word.

target_texts.text: Good words are honeycombs, and their sweetness is healing of the life.

rationale: The receptive ear makes a wise word precious; 15:32 likewise says the person who keeps rebukes loves his own life rather than rejecting discipline.
source_text: A costly carnelian is fastened into a golden earring—a wise word into a receptive ear.

target_texts.text: One who thrusts discipline away hates himself, but one who keeps rebukes loves his own life.

rationale: Both praise a faithful messenger's benefit to the sender: refreshment in the harvest-heat comparison here, and rescue of a rash king in 13:17.
source_text: As snow coming forth benefits people in harvest heat, so a faithful messenger benefits those who sent him; for he benefits the lives of those who employ him.

target_texts.text: A rash king will fall into evils, but a faithful messenger will rescue him.

rationale: A soft tongue has surprising power here; 15:1 explains that a yielding answer turns away wrath rather than intensifying it.
source_text: In patience is prosperity for kings, and a soft tongue crushes bones.

target_texts.text: Anger destroys even intelligent people; but a yielding answer turns away wrath, and a painful word stirs up anger.

rationale: Both explicitly limit honey consumption: 25:16 warns that excess makes one vomit, and 25:27 states that eating much honey is not good.
source_text: Having found honey, eat what is sufficient, lest you become full and vomit.

target_texts.text: Eating much honey is not good, but one must honor glorious words.

rationale: False testimony is compared to a club, sword, and arrow here; 12:18 likewise describes speech that wounds like a sword.
source_text: A club and sword and barbed arrow—so also is a man testifying false testimony against his friend.

target_texts.text: There are those who wound with a sword as they speak, but the tongues of the wise heal.

rationale: This native saying connects bodily suffering with pain of heart; 17:22 similarly links sorrow with bodily harm, describing a sorrowful person's drying bones.
source_text: As vinegar is unsuitable for a wound, so a suffering that falls upon the body pains the heart.

target_texts.text: A rejoicing heart makes one flourish, but a sorrowful man’s bones dry up.

rationale: Grief harms the heart as moth and worm damage materials; 17:22 describes sorrow drying a person's bones, another image of inward distress harming bodily life.
source_text: As a moth harms a garment and a worm wood, so a man’s grief harms the heart.

target_texts.text: A rejoicing heart makes one flourish, but a sorrowful man’s bones dry up.

rationale: Romans repeats the instruction to feed a hungry enemy and give a thirsty enemy drink, then carries forward the coals-of-fire explanation.
source_text: If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink;

target_texts.text: But if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him a drink; for by doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head.

rationale: Romans reproduces the image of heaping fiery coals on an enemy's head through feeding and giving drink; Proverbs additionally states the Lord's good repayment.
source_text: for by doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head, and the Lord will repay you good things.

target_texts.text: But if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him a drink; for by doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head.

rationale: Both prefer an inhospitable dwelling to sharing a home with a contentious wife: a roof corner here and desert country in 21:19.
source_text: Better to dwell on a corner of a roof than with an abusive wife in a shared house.

target_texts.text: Better to dwell in a desert land than with a battling, talkative, and quick-tempered woman.

rationale: Welcome news refreshes like cold water here; 15:30 likewise gives a good report a bodily effect, making bones full.
source_text: As cold water is welcome to a thirsty life, so is good news from a faraway land.

target_texts.text: An eye looking at good things gladdens the heart, and a good report makes bones full.

rationale: The judgment that much honey is not good returns to the earlier warning to eat only a sufficient amount and avoid sickness from excess.
source_text: Eating much honey is not good, but one must honor glorious words.

target_texts.text: Having found honey, eat what is sufficient, lest you become full and vomit.

rationale: The native proverb compares acting without counsel to an unwalled city; 11:14 similarly contrasts falling without steering with deliverance through much counsel.
source_text: As a city with its walls cast down and unwalled, so is a man who does something without counsel.

target_texts.text: Those who have no steering fall like leaves, but deliverance is in much counsel.

rationale: Both insist that honoring a fool is inappropriate, first by dew at harvest and rain in summer and then by a stone bound in a sling.
source_text: Like dew at harvest and rain in summer, so honor does not belong to a fool.

target_texts.text: One who binds a stone in a sling is like one who gives glory to a fool.

rationale: An empty curse lands on no one here; Balaam likewise refuses to presume that he can effectively curse someone whom God does not curse.
source_text: As birds and sparrows fly, so an empty curse will come upon no one.

target_texts.text: Why should I curse whom the Lord does not curse? Why should I call down a curse on whom God does not curse?

rationale: The rod for a lawless nation resembles the whips and shoulder punishments prepared for the undisciplined and foolish in 19:29.
source_text: As a whip for a horse and a goad for a donkey, so a rod for a lawless nation.

target_texts.text: Whips are prepared for the undisciplined, and punishments for the shoulders of fools.

rationale: Both caution against speaking to folly on its own terms: here the danger is becoming like the fool, while 23:9 anticipates contempt for intelligent words.
source_text: Do not answer a fool in relation to his foolishness, so that you do not become like him;

target_texts.text: Say nothing into a fool’s ears, lest he sneer at your intelligent words.

rationale: The paired commands give different reasons for responding to folly: avoid becoming like the fool, yet expose foolishness when silence would confirm self-conceit.
source_text: but answer a fool according to his foolishness, so that he does not appear wise to himself.

target_texts.text: Do not answer a fool in relation to his foolishness, so that you do not become like him;

rationale: A foolish messenger brings the sender reproach here, whereas 13:17 credits a faithful messenger with rescuing the king who sends him.
source_text: One who sends a word through a foolish messenger will drink reproach from his own feet.

target_texts.text: A rash king will fall into evils, but a faithful messenger will rescue him.

rationale: Removing a proverb from a fool's mouth corresponds to withholding intelligent words from a fool's ears; both portray wisdom as mishandled by folly.
source_text: Remove walking from legs, and a proverb from the mouth of fools.

target_texts.text: Say nothing into a fool’s ears, lest he sneer at your intelligent words.

rationale: The stone bound in a sling represents misplaced honor for a fool, matching the earlier comparison of such honor to dew at harvest and rain in summer.
source_text: One who binds a stone in a sling is like one who gives glory to a fool.

target_texts.text: Like dew at harvest and rain in summer, so honor does not belong to a fool.

rationale: Peter explicitly calls the dog's return to its vomit a true proverb and applies it to returning to defilement, matching Proverbs' return to one's own sin.
source_text: Like a dog that comes upon its own vomit and becomes hateful is a fool who has returned in his own wickedness to his own sin.

target_texts.text: What the true proverb says has happened to them: “A dog has returned to its own vomit,” and, “A sow, after washing, returns to wallowing in mud.”

rationale: Both distinguish shame that produces sin from shame that brings glory and favor, using the same two-part moral distinction.
source_text: There is shame that brings on sin, and there is shame that is glory and favor.

target_texts.text: For there is shame that brings sin, and there is shame that is glory and favor.

rationale: The person who thinks himself wise is worse off than a fool; 3:7 directly warns against being prudent in one's own estimation.
source_text: I saw a man who thought himself wise, yet a fool had more hope than he.

target_texts.text: Do not be prudent in your own estimation; fear God and turn away from every evil.

rationale: Both give the lazy person's excuse that a lion is in the roads; 22:13 expands it with imagined murderers in the squares.
source_text: A lazy person sent on a journey says, “A lion is in the roads!”

target_texts.text: The lazy person makes an excuse and says, “A lion is in the roads, and murderers in the squares!”

rationale: The lazy person turns on the bed like a door on hinges; 6:9-10 likewise rebukes remaining asleep instead of getting up.
source_text: As a door turns on its hinge, so a lazy person on his bed.

target_texts.text: How long will you remain lying down, sluggard? When will you rise from sleep?
You sleep a little, sit a little, doze a little, and clasp your chest with your hands a little;

rationale: Both picture a person hiding a hand in the lap and failing even to bring it to the mouth, presenting inactivity as self-defeating.
source_text: A lazy person, having hidden his hand in his lap, will not be able to bring it to his mouth.

target_texts.text: One who unjustly hides his hands in his lap will certainly not even bring them to his mouth.

rationale: The lazy person's estimate of his own superior wisdom exemplifies the self-conceit already judged more hopeless than ordinary folly in 26:12.
source_text: The lazy person appears wiser to himself than one who brings back a message in full.

target_texts.text: I saw a man who thought himself wise, yet a fool had more hope than he.

rationale: Interfering in another's dispute is as hazardous as grabbing a dog's tail; 3:30 likewise warns against provoking needless enmity and the harm it can bring.
source_text: As one who grasps a dog’s tail, so is one who presides over another’s dispute.

target_texts.text: Do not seek enmity with anyone in vain, lest he do you some harm.

rationale: Ambushing a friend and excusing it as play violates the earlier prohibition against devising evil toward a trusting friend who lives nearby.
source_text: so are all who ambush their own friends, and when detected say, “I did it in play.”

target_texts.text: Do not devise evils against your friend who lives nearby and trusts in you.

rationale: Removing the person who fuels conflict quiets battle here; 22:10 likewise says that expelling a pestilent person sends strife out of the council.
source_text: With much wood a fire flourishes, but where there is no double-minded person, battle is quiet.

target_texts.text: Cast a pestilent person out of a council, and strife will go out with him; for whenever he sits in a council, he dishonors everyone.

rationale: The abusive person feeds battle as wood feeds fire; 15:18 similarly identifies the quick-tempered person as the one who prepares battles.
source_text: A hearth for coals and wood for fire, and an abusive man for the turmoil of battle.

target_texts.text: A quick-tempered man prepares battles, but a patient person calms even a battle about to begin.

rationale: Soft words strike the inward parts here; 5:3-4 likewise contrasts seductive honey-sweet speech with its later bitterness and cutting harm.
source_text: The words of tricksters are soft, but they strike into the store-chambers of the inward parts.

target_texts.text: Do not attend to a base woman, for honey drips from a prostitute’s lips; for a time she oils your throat.
Afterward, however, you will find it more bitter than gall and sharper than a two-edged blade.

rationale: Smooth lips conceal a painful heart here; the next portrait makes the mismatch explicit in an enemy whose agreeing lips conceal inward deceit.
source_text: Silver given with deceit must be regarded like a potsherd; smooth lips cover a painful heart.

target_texts.text: A weeping enemy agrees to everything with his lips, but in his heart devises deceits;

rationale: The enemy's outward agreement conceals deceit; the following warning explains why a loud entreaty should not persuade the hearer when inward evils remain.
source_text: A weeping enemy agrees to everything with his lips, but in his heart devises deceits;

target_texts.text: if the enemy entreats you with a loud voice, do not be persuaded, for seven evils are in his life.

rationale: Refusing to trust an enemy's entreaties without considering the hidden evils accords with the resourceful person's reconsideration instead of believing every word.
source_text: if the enemy entreats you with a loud voice, do not be persuaded, for seven evils are in his life.

target_texts.text: The innocent person believes every word, but the resourceful comes to reconsideration.

rationale: Concealed enmity establishes deceit here; 26:24 supplies the closely related portrait of an enemy whose agreeable lips hide a heart devising deceits.
source_text: One who hides enmity establishes deceit, but one well known in councils discloses his own sins.

target_texts.text: A weeping enemy agrees to everything with his lips, but in his heart devises deceits;

rationale: Both describe the digger falling into his own pit; Proverbs explicitly directs the pit against a neighbor and adds the returning stone.
source_text: One who digs a pit for his neighbor will fall into it, and one who rolls a stone rolls it upon himself.

target_texts.text: Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and whoever tears down a fence will be bitten by a snake.

rationale: The false tongue is opposed to truth here; 12:22 locates the same moral divide in the Lord's rejection of lying lips and approval of faithful deeds.
source_text: A false tongue hates truth, but an unrestrained mouth makes disorders.

target_texts.text: Lying lips are an abomination to the Lord, but one who performs faithful deeds is acceptable to Him.

rationale: Both forbid confident boasting about tomorrow because its events are unknown; James applies that limit to plans for travel, trade, and profit.
source_text: Do not boast of things for tomorrow, for you do not know what the coming day will bear.

target_texts.text: Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go to this city, spend a year there, trade, and make a profit”—
you who do not know what tomorrow brings. What is your life? For you are a vapor, appearing for a little while and then disappearing.
Instead, you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we shall both live and do this or that.”
But now you boast in your pretensions. All such boasting is evil.

rationale: Praise should come from another rather than one's own mouth; Paul likewise denies that self-commendation establishes approval and points to the Lord's commendation.
source_text: Let your neighbor praise you, and not your mouth, another, and not your lips.

target_texts.text: For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.

rationale: Jealousy is portrayed as bearing with no one; the earlier account of a jealous husband similarly describes wrath that refuses ransom or reconciliation.
source_text: Wrath is merciless and anger sharp, but jealousy bears with no one.

target_texts.text: For her husband’s anger is full of jealousy; he will not spare on the day of judgment,
he will not trade his enmity for any ransom, nor be reconciled by many gifts.

rationale: Open correction is valued above concealed friendship; 28:23 similarly ranks candid reproof above flattering words in the favor it ultimately wins.
source_text: Open rebukes are better than concealed friendship.

target_texts.text: One who reproves a person’s ways will have more favor than one who flatters with the tongue.

rationale: The proverb distrusts an enemy's willing kisses; Judas' kiss to identify Jesus for arrest supplies a concrete instance of affectionate appearance used for betrayal.
source_text: A friend’s wounds are more trustworthy than an enemy’s willing kisses.

target_texts.text: The one handing Him over had given them a sign, saying, “The One I kiss is He; seize Him.”
Immediately he came to Jesus and said, “Greetings, Rabbi,” and kissed Him.
Jesus said to him, “Friend, do what you have come for.” Then they came forward, laid their hands upon Jesus, and seized Him.

rationale: Misfortunes tear the life apart despite pleasures that delight the heart; 17:22 likewise describes sorrow's destructive effect on the person's bodily life.
source_text: The heart delights in perfumes and wines and incense, but the life is torn apart by misfortunes.

target_texts.text: A rejoicing heart makes one flourish, but a sorrowful man’s bones dry up.

rationale: Both emphasize durable friendship in times of need; 27:10 particularly values a nearby friend, while 17:17 calls for friendship at all times.
source_text: Do not abandon your friend or an ancestral friend, and do not enter your brother’s house when misfortune strikes you; a nearby friend is better than a brother dwelling far away.

target_texts.text: Let a friend be yours at all times, and let brothers be useful in times of need; for this is why they are born.

rationale: The son's wisdom makes the speaker's heart rejoice in both passages; 23:16 further connects that shared joy with upright speech.
source_text: Become wise, son, so that my heart may rejoice, and turn reproachful words away from yourself.

target_texts.text: Son, if your heart becomes wise, you will gladden my heart too,
and your lips will spend time in words with my lips, if the words are upright.

rationale: Both contrast the resourceful person's response to observed danger with fools who continue onward and suffer a penalty.
source_text: A resourceful person hid when evils approached, but fools who went on will pay a penalty.

target_texts.text: A resourceful person, seeing an evil person severely punished, is himself instructed, but fools passed by and were penalized.

rationale: The abusive wife drives a man from his house like winter dripping; 21:19 similarly regards desert dwelling as preferable to life with a contentious wife.
source_text: Drops drive a man from his house on a wintry day, and likewise an abusive wife from his own house.

target_texts.text: Better to dwell in a desert land than with a battling, talkative, and quick-tempered woman.

rationale: The person who plants a fig tree eats its fruit; Paul similarly appeals to the vineyard planter's right to eat the fruit of his labor.
source_text: One who plants a fig tree will eat its fruits, and one who guards his own master will be honored.

target_texts.text: Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat its fruit? Who shepherds a flock and does not share in the flock’s milk?

rationale: Both describe the eye as never filled; Proverbs places human visual desire beside the insatiability of Hades and destruction.
source_text: Hades and destruction are not filled, and likewise human eyes are insatiable.

target_texts.text: All words are wearisome; a man will not be able to speak. The eye will not be filled with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.

rationale: The condemned fixing of an eye recalls the malicious man's eye signals in 6:13-14, where bodily gestures accompany a heart devising evil.
source_text: One who fixes an eye is an abomination to the Lord, and the uneducated are unrestrained in tongue.

target_texts.text: the same man signals with his eye and gives signs with his foot, and instructs by gestures of his fingers;
with a twisted heart he devises evils at every time. Such a person stirs up disturbances for a city.

rationale: Both compare human evaluation with testing silver and gold; 27:21 names praise as the human test, while 17:3 places the choosing of hearts before the Lord.
source_text: A test for silver and gold is burning, but a man is tested through the mouth of those who praise him.

target_texts.text: As silver and gold are tested in a furnace, so hearts are chosen before the Lord.

rationale: Both contrast an upright heart's pursuit of discernment or knowledge with the evil orientation of the uneducated or lawless.
source_text: A lawless person’s heart searches out evils, but an upright heart searches out knowledge.

target_texts.text: An upright heart seeks discernment, but the mouth of the uneducated will know evil things.

rationale: Both say that whipping fails to remove a fool's lack of understanding; 17:10 contrasts this with the intelligent person's responsiveness even to a threat.
source_text: If you whip a fool in the midst of a council, dishonoring him, you will certainly not strip away his foolishness.

target_texts.text: A threat crushes an intelligent person’s heart, but a fool, though whipped, does not perceive.

rationale: Attentive knowledge of the flock's lives accords with the righteous person's compassion for the lives of his animals in 12:10.
source_text: Know thoroughly the lives of your flock, and set your heart upon your herds;

target_texts.text: The righteous has compassion on the lives of his animals, but the inward affections of the impious are merciless.

rationale: Gathering grass and mountain fodder for livestock reflects the same timely provision commended in the ant's preparation of food during summer and harvest.
source_text: Care for the green growth in the plain, and you will cut grass, and gather mountain fodder,

target_texts.text: it prepares its food in summer and makes abundant provision at harvest.

rationale: The native verse offers strong sayings for the life of the son and attendants; 4:20-22 likewise says retained words give life and healing to those who find them.
source_text: Son, from me you have strong sayings for your life, and for the life of your attendants.

target_texts.text: Son, attend to my utterance; apply your ear to my words,
so that your springs do not fail you; keep them in your heart,
for there is life for those who find them and healing for all flesh.

rationale: The impious person's flight when nobody pursues repeats the striking image used in Leviticus for the fear accompanying judgment.
source_text: An impious person flees when no one pursues, but a righteous person is confident like a lion.

target_texts.text: And I will set My face against you, and you shall fall before your enemies. Those who hate you shall pursue you, and you shall flee when no one pursues you.

rationale: Both contrast those who create disputes with the prudent or patient person who extinguishes them.
source_text: Through the sins of the impious, disputes arise, but a prudent man will extinguish them.

target_texts.text: A patient man will extinguish disputes, but the impious stirs them up still more.

rationale: The vigorous evildoer's extortion of the poor is judged explicitly in 14:31 as an offense against the poor person's Maker.
source_text: A man vigorous in impieties extorts the poor. Just like a violent and useless rain,

target_texts.text: One who extorts from the needy provokes the One who made him, but one who honors Him has mercy on the poor.

rationale: Loving the law surrounds people with a wall here; 19:16 similarly makes keeping a command a protection for one's own life.
source_text: so those who abandon the law praise impiety, but those who love the law surround themselves with a wall.

target_texts.text: One who keeps a command guards his own life, but one who despises his own ways will perish.

rationale: Those who seek the Lord gain understanding of judgment; 2:5-9 likewise connects finding God's knowledge with understanding righteousness and judgment.
source_text: Evil men will not understand judgment, but those who seek the Lord will understand in everything.

target_texts.text: then you will understand the fear of the Lord and find the knowledge of God.
For the Lord gives wisdom, and from His presence come knowledge and understanding.
He stores up salvation for those acting rightly; He will shield their journey,
to guard the ways of righteous ordinances, and He will protect the way of those who revere Him.
Then you will understand righteousness and judgment, and you will make all good courses straight.

rationale: Both explicitly prefer a righteous or truthful poor person to a wealthy liar, ranking integrity above possessions.
source_text: Better a poor person walking in truth than a lying rich person.

target_texts.text: Mercy is a man’s fruit, and better a righteous poor person than a rich liar.

rationale: The understanding son's keeping of law contrasts with conduct that dishonors a father; 13:1 similarly pairs a resourceful son's obedience with the disobedient son's destruction.
source_text: An understanding son keeps the law, but one who tends dissipation dishonors a father.

target_texts.text: A resourceful son is obedient to a father, but a disobedient son is in destruction.

rationale: Wealth gained by interest and gains is ultimately gathered for someone merciful to the poor; 13:22 similarly stores the impious person's wealth for the righteous.
source_text: One who increases his wealth with interest and gains gathers it for one who shows mercy to the poor.

target_texts.text: A good man will inherit children’s children, but the wealth of the impious is stored up for the righteous.

rationale: Turning away from the law compromises prayer here; Isaiah likewise joins God's refusal of supplication with a demand to cease wrongdoing and practice justice.
source_text: One who turns his ear aside so as not to hear the law has himself also abhorred his own prayer.

target_texts.text: Whenever you stretch your hands toward Me, I will turn My eyes away from you. Even if you multiply supplication, I will not listen to you, for your hands are full of blood.
Wash yourselves, become clean. Remove the evils from your souls, before My eyes. Stop your evil deeds.
Learn to do good, seek judgment, rescue the wronged. Give judgment for the orphan and vindicate the widow.

rationale: The person who leads the upright into an evil way falls into destruction himself; 26:27 similarly makes a trap intended for a neighbor recoil on its maker.
source_text: One who leads the upright astray on an evil way will himself fall into destruction; but the lawless will pass by good things and will not enter into them.

target_texts.text: One who digs a pit for his neighbor will fall into it, and one who rolls a stone rolls it upon himself.

rationale: The rich man's inflated estimate of his wisdom is challenged here; First Timothy directly warns the rich against arrogance and misplaced confidence in wealth.
source_text: A rich man is wise in his own estimation, but an intelligent poor person will judge him.

target_texts.text: Command those who are rich in the present age not to be arrogant nor to set their hope on the uncertainty of wealth, but on God, who richly provides us all things for enjoyment,

rationale: Both contrast the communal benefit brought by righteous people with the public harm caused by the impious: glory versus capture here, prosperity versus a razed city there.
source_text: Through the help of the righteous much glory comes about, but in the places of the impious people are captured.

target_texts.text: Through the good things of the righteous a city prospered,
but by the mouths of the impious it was razed.

rationale: The native text says one who explains reproofs will be loved; 9:8 likewise says that reproving a wise person elicits love. The link does not substitute a confession-and-mercy wording.
source_text: One who covers his own impiety will not prosper, but one who explains reproofs will be loved.

target_texts.text: Do not reprove evil people, so that they may not hate you; reprove a wise person, and he will love you.

rationale: Both warn of the hard heart's bad outcome: falling into evils here and failing to encounter good things in 17:20.
source_text: Happy is a man who shrinks from everything out of reverence, but one hard of heart will fall into evils.

target_texts.text: but one hard of heart does not meet good things. A man changeable in tongue will fall into evils,

rationale: The tyrant over a needy nation is a hungry lion and thirsty wolf; Ezekiel likewise portrays exploitative leaders as devouring lions and predatory wolves.
source_text: One who tyrannizes over a needy nation while himself poor is a hungry lion and a thirsty wolf.

target_texts.text: Her leaders within her are like roaring lions seizing prey, devouring lives with power, taking payments unjustly, and your widows have multiplied within you.

Her priests set aside My law and profaned My holy things. They did not distinguish between holy and profane, nor distinguish between unclean and clean. They covered their eyes from My Sabbaths, and I was profaned among them.
Her rulers within her are like wolves seizing prey to shed blood, so that in greed they may gain more.

rationale: The king who hates injustice is promised life, in contrast to extortion; 15:27 likewise opposes destructive bribe-taking to the safety of rejecting unjust gifts.
source_text: A king lacking revenues is a great extortioner, but one who hates injustice will live a long time.

target_texts.text: One who takes bribes destroys himself, but one who hates taking gifts is saved.

rationale: Both command discipline of a son and promise that he will adorn the parent's life; 28:17a speaks of love and 29:17 of rest.
source_text: Discipline a son, and he will love you and give adornment to your life; you must not heed a lawless nation.

target_texts.text: Discipline your son, and he will give you rest and give adornment to your life.

rationale: Righteous walking brings help while crooked walking entangles; 11:5-6 similarly connects straight righteous paths with rescue and lawlessness with self-entrapment.
source_text: One who walks righteously has been helped, but one who walks crooked ways will become entangled.

target_texts.text: Righteousness cuts blameless paths straight, but impiety falls into injustice.
The righteousness of upright men rescues them, but lawless people are caught in their own destruction.

rationale: Both promise bread to the person who works his own land and criticize pursuing empty leisure instead of productive work.
source_text: One who works his own land will be filled with bread, but one who pursues leisure will be filled with poverty.

target_texts.text: One who works his own land will be filled with loaves, but those who pursue empty things lack understanding.

rationale: Selling a man for a morsel of bread resembles Amos' condemnation of selling the righteous for silver and the poor for sandals: human justice is sacrificed for gain.
source_text: One who has no respect for the faces of the righteous is not good; such a person will sell a man for a morsel of bread.

target_texts.text: Thus says the Lord: “For three impieties of Israel, and for four, I will not turn away from him, because they sold a righteous person for silver and a poor person for sandals,

rationale: The grudging person's haste to become rich is set beside Paul's warning that desire for riches leads to temptation, snares, and ruin.
source_text: A grudging man hastens to become rich and does not know that a merciful person will rule over him.

target_texts.text: But those who want to become rich fall into temptation and a snare and many foolish and harmful desires, which plunge people into ruin and destruction.

rationale: The reprover gains more favor than the flatterer; 9:8 likewise says a wise person responds to reproof with love.
source_text: One who reproves a person’s ways will have more favor than one who flatters with the tongue.

target_texts.text: Do not reprove evil people, so that they may not hate you; reprove a wise person, and he will love you.

rationale: Casting away father or mother while denying sin is condemned here; 19:26 similarly condemns dishonoring a father and thrusting a mother away.
source_text: One who casts away a father or mother and thinks he is not sinning is a partner of an impious man.

target_texts.text: One who dishonors a father and thrusts his mother away will be put to shame and be subject to reproach.

rationale: Trust in the Lord offers care in contrast to the insatiable person's rash judgment; 3:5 likewise directs confidence toward God instead of one's own wisdom.
source_text: An insatiable man judges rashly, but one who trusts in the Lord will be cared for.

target_texts.text: Trust God with your whole heart; do not exalt yourself in your own wisdom.

rationale: Trusting a rash heart is foolish here; 3:5-7 likewise rejects self-reliance in wisdom and calls for trust in God, reverence, and turning from evil.
source_text: One who trusts in a rash heart is a fool; but one who walks in wisdom will be saved.

target_texts.text: Trust God with your whole heart; do not exalt yourself in your own wisdom.
In all your ways acknowledge her, that she may cut your ways straight; and your foot will surely not stumble.
Do not be prudent in your own estimation; fear God and turn away from every evil.

rationale: Both associate provision for the poor with provision for the giver: freedom from need here, and nourishment for the one sharing bread in 22:9.
source_text: One who gives to the poor will not be in need; but one who turns away his eye will be in great difficulty.

target_texts.text: One who has mercy on the poor will himself be nourished, for he gave of his own loaves to the poor.

rationale: The righteous groan under impious dominance here; 29:2 similarly says people groan when the impious rule and rejoice when the righteous are praised.
source_text: In the places of the impious the righteous groan, but at their destruction the righteous will multiply.

target_texts.text: When the righteous are praised, peoples will rejoice; but when the impious rule, men groan.

rationale: The stiff-necked person's sudden burning has no healing; 6:15 likewise describes the malicious person's sudden destruction as an incurable crushing.
source_text: Better a man who reproves than a stiff-necked man; for when the latter suddenly burns, there is no healing.

target_texts.text: Therefore his destruction comes suddenly: a cutting down and an incurable crushing,

rationale: The groaning under impious rule matches the righteous person's groaning in places dominated by the impious in 28:28.
source_text: When the righteous are praised, peoples will rejoice; but when the impious rule, men groan.

target_texts.text: In the places of the impious the righteous groan, but at their destruction the righteous will multiply.

rationale: The father's joy when his son loves wisdom restates 10:1's declaration that a wise son makes a father glad.
source_text: When a man loves wisdom, his father rejoices; but one who tends prostitutes will destroy wealth.

target_texts.text: A wise son makes a father glad, but a foolish son is grief to his mother.

rationale: A righteous king raises up a country while lawlessness tears it down; 14:34 similarly says righteousness exalts a nation and sins diminish peoples.
source_text: A righteous king raises up a country, but a lawless man tears it down.

target_texts.text: Righteousness exalts a nation, but sins diminish tribes.

rationale: A net prepared for a friend entangles the setter's own feet; 26:27 likewise makes the neighbor-directed pit and stone recoil on their maker.
source_text: One who prepares a net before his own friend’s face wraps it around his own feet.

target_texts.text: One who digs a pit for his neighbor will fall into it, and one who rolls a stone rolls it upon himself.

rationale: The sinning person encounters a great snare; 5:22 likewise says lawless deeds hunt their doer and one's own sins become binding cords.
source_text: For a sinning man there is a great snare, but a righteous person will be in joy and gladness.

target_texts.text: Lawless acts hunt a man, and each is bound tight by the cords of his own sins.

rationale: The righteous person's ability to judge for the needy corresponds to the royal instruction to judge justly and decide the poor and weak person's case.
source_text: A righteous person knows how to judge for the needy, but the impious person will not understand knowledge, and a poor person has no discerning mind.

target_texts.text: Open your mouth and judge justly, and decide the case of the poor and weak.

rationale: Wise people turn away the wrath that destructive people inflame; 15:18 likewise opposes a patient peacemaker to the quick-tempered instigator of battle.
source_text: Pestilent men set a city ablaze, but wise people turned away wrath.

target_texts.text: A quick-tempered man prepares battles, but a patient person calms even a battle about to begin.

rationale: The wise person controls the release of anger instead of pouring it all out; 17:27 similarly commends withholding harsh words and patient understanding.
source_text: A fool brings out all his anger, but a wise person stores it up portion by portion.

target_texts.text: One who refrains from sending forth a harsh word is discerning, and a patient man is intelligent.

rationale: A king's willingness to hear unjust speech corrupts those under him; 17:4 likewise associates evil with listening to lawless tongues and righteousness with rejecting lies.
source_text: When a king listens to an unjust word, all those under him are lawless.

target_texts.text: An evil person heeds the tongue of lawless people, but a righteous person pays no attention to lying lips.

rationale: The Lord inspects lender and debtor together here; 22:2 similarly brings rich and poor together before the Lord who made both, placing unequal parties under one divine regard.
source_text: When lender and debtor come together, the Lord inspects both.

target_texts.text: Rich and poor met one another, and the Lord made both.

rationale: A throne is established through truthful judgment of the poor here; 16:12 likewise grounds a throne's preparation in righteousness rather than evil.
source_text: When a king judges the poor in truth, his throne will be established as a testimony.

target_texts.text: One who does evil is an abomination to a king, for a throne of rule is prepared with righteousness.

rationale: Blows and reproofs are presented as formative discipline; 13:24 likewise associates careful correction of a son with parental love rather than neglect.
source_text: Blows and reproofs give wisdom, but a wandering child shames his parents.

target_texts.text: One who spares the staff hates his son, but one who loves him disciplines carefully.

rationale: Both tell a parent to discipline a son and promise adornment of the parent's life, with rest here and the son's love in 28:17a.
source_text: Discipline your son, and he will give you rest and give adornment to your life.

target_texts.text: Discipline a son, and he will love you and give adornment to your life; you must not heed a lawless nation.

rationale: The blessing attached to keeping the law corresponds to the preservation of life attached to keeping a command in 19:16.
source_text: There will certainly be no interpreter for a lawless nation, but one who keeps the law is blessed.

target_texts.text: One who keeps a command guards his own life, but one who despises his own ways will perish.

rationale: Hasty speech is more hopeless than folly here; 18:13 gives a concrete case, calling an answer delivered before listening foolish and reproachful.
source_text: If you see a man swift in words, know that a fool has more hope than he.

target_texts.text: One who answers a word before hearing it—it is foolishness and reproach for him.

rationale: Both identify the angry person as an originator of strife or battle, making uncontrolled anger productive of further wrongdoing.
source_text: A wrathful man digs up strife, and an angry man dug out sins.

target_texts.text: A quick-tempered man prepares battles, but a patient person calms even a battle about to begin.

rationale: Insolence brings humiliation while the Lord supports the humble with glory; 3:34 likewise contrasts divine opposition to pride with grace for the humble.
source_text: Insolence brings a man low, but the Lord supports the humble-minded with glory.

target_texts.text: The Lord opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.

rationale: The warning about a hearer who fails to report when an oath is imposed corresponds to Leviticus' rule that a knowledgeable witness who does not declare the matter bears sin.
source_text: One who shares with a thief hates his own life; but if, when an oath is set before them, those who heard do not report,

target_texts.text: And if a soul sins, and hears the voice of a solemn adjuration, and he is a witness, whether he has seen or has knowledge of the matter, if he does not declare it, he shall bear the sin.

rationale: Fear and shame before people become a trap, whereas trust in the Master saves; 7:1a likewise tells the son to honor the Lord and fear no other apart from Him.
source_text: having feared and felt shame before people, they were tripped up; but one who trusts in the Lord will rejoice. Impiety gives a man a fall; but one who trusts in the Master will be saved.

target_texts.text: Son, honor the Lord and you will be strong; apart from Him, fear no other.

rationale: Justice for a person comes from the Lord despite the pursuit of leaders' favor; the native 16:33 likewise says all righteous things are from the Lord.
source_text: Many court the faces of leaders, but what is just for a man comes from the Lord.

target_texts.text: Everything comes into the laps of the unjust, but all righteous things are from the Lord.

rationale: The righteous reject injustice while the lawless reject a straightening way; 15:9 aligns the Lord with righteousness by calling impious ways an abomination to Him.
source_text: An unjust man is an abomination to the righteous, but a straightening way is an abomination to a lawless person.

target_texts.text: The ways of the impious are an abomination to the Lord, but He loves those who pursue righteousness.

rationale: Both praise a courageous woman; 31:10 values her above costly stones, while 12:4 portrays her as a crown to her husband.
source_text: A courageous woman—who will find her? Such a woman is more precious than costly stones.

target_texts.text: A courageous woman is a crown to her husband; but as a worm in wood, so a woman who does evil destroys a man.

rationale: The husband's confidence and benefit from his wife correspond to Sirach's description of a wife's grace and knowledge delighting and strengthening her husband.
source_text: Her husband’s heart is confident in her; such a woman will not lack fine spoils.

target_texts.text: A wife’s grace will delight her husband, and her knowledge will fatten his bones.

rationale: The wife's lifelong good toward her husband corresponds to the courageous wife who gladdens him and enables years completed in peace.
source_text: For she works good things for her husband throughout her life.

target_texts.text: A courageous wife gladdens her husband, and he will complete his years in peace.

rationale: The woman's productive textile work resembles Dorcas' making of tunics and garments, recalled by the widows as concrete evidence of her service.
source_text: Spinning wool and flax, she made useful work with her hands.

target_texts.text: Peter rose and went with them. When he arrived, they brought him into the upper room. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing the tunics and garments Dorcas had made while she was with them.

rationale: Providing food for the household and assigning servants their work resembles the prudent steward's responsibility to distribute the household staff's ration at the proper time.
source_text: And she rises in the night and gave food to the household and tasks to the maidservants.

target_texts.text: And the Lord said, “Who, then, is the faithful steward, the prudent one, whom his master will appoint over his household staff to give out their ration of grain at the proper time?

rationale: The woman braces her arms for work; 13:4 similarly contrasts idle desire with the courageous person's hands actively engaged in care.
source_text: Having girded her waist strongly, she braced her arms for work.

target_texts.text: Every idle person is amid desires, but the hands of the courageous are engaged in care.

rationale: The woman recognizes work's benefit and continues through the night; 14:23 likewise associates attentive labor with abundance and pleasure-seeking inactivity with want.
source_text: She tasted that working is good, and her lamp is not extinguished throughout the night.

target_texts.text: In everyone who takes care there is abundance, but the pleasure-loving and unfeeling person will be in want.

rationale: The hands working a spindle belong to the same practical sphere as Dorcas' garment-making, where skilled handwork becomes useful provision for others.
source_text: She stretches her forearms toward profitable things, and braces her hands on a spindle.

target_texts.text: Peter rose and went with them. When he arrived, they brought him into the upper room. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing the tunics and garments Dorcas had made while she was with them.

rationale: Her hands are opened to the needy and poor; 19:17 explicitly commends mercy toward the poor as a gift whose repayment the Lord undertakes.
source_text: She opened her hands to a needy person and stretched out her wrist to a poor person.

target_texts.text: One who has mercy on the poor lends to God, and He will repay him according to his gift.

rationale: Her household is adequately clothed, relieving her husband's anxiety; First Timothy similarly treats provision for one's own household as a serious obligation.
source_text: Her husband is not anxious about those at home when he stays away somewhere, for all those with her are clothed.

target_texts.text: But if someone does not provide for his own, and especially his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.

rationale: The husband's distinction among elders forms part of the portrait of the capable wife; 12:4 likewise calls a courageous woman her husband's crown.
source_text: Her husband becomes distinguished in the gates when he sits in council with the elder inhabitants of the land.

target_texts.text: A courageous woman is a crown to her husband; but as a worm in wood, so a woman who does evil destroys a man.

rationale: The native verse describes attentive, lawful speech and a tongue kept in order; 13:3 likewise connects guarding the mouth with preservation of life.
source_text: She opened her mouth attentively and lawfully and prescribed order for her tongue.

target_texts.text: One who guards his own mouth keeps his own life, but one rash with his lips will terrify himself.

rationale: Her secure household occupations and refusal of idle food correspond to 12:11's contrast between working one's land for bread and pursuing empty things.
source_text: The occupations of her houses are secure, and she did not eat idle food.

target_texts.text: One who works his own land will be filled with loaves, but those who pursue empty things lack understanding.

rationale: The woman's mercy in raising her children belongs with First Timothy's commendation of child-rearing, assistance to the afflicted, and a life attested by good works.
source_text: She opens her mouth wisely and according to law, and her mercy raised up her children, and they became wealthy, and her husband praised her:

target_texts.text: attested for good works: if she brought up children, if she received strangers, if she washed saints’ feet, if she assisted the afflicted, if she followed every good work.

rationale: Proverbs ranks understanding and fear of the Lord above pleasing appearance; Peter similarly values the inward character of women who hope in God above outward adornment.
source_text: A woman’s pleasing qualities are false and beauty is vain; for an understanding woman is blessed, and let her praise the fear of the Lord.

target_texts.text: Let your adornment not be the outward kind—braiding hair, putting on gold ornaments, or dressing in garments—
but the hidden person of the heart, in the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is very precious before God.
For this is how the holy women of former times, who hoped in God, also adorned themselves, submitting themselves to their own husbands,
